evidence.quote: We gathered a corpus of 144 dashboards by starting with the 83 dashboards collected by Sarikaya et al. [44] but discarding three due to lack of clarity or context.
We then added 64 new dashboards found on news websites and personal applications. 36 of these dashboards were related to Covid-19 due to recent public interest.

Three of the authors then created independent coding schemes by qualitatively analyzing the dashboards in the corpus using the constant comparative method [22]. Where available, we coded the interactive version of the dashboard (61%).
These schemes were refined and consolidated with the help of another three additional coders not involved in the initial scheme.

Thresholds (21%) indicate states and values that bear some meaning, such as ‘good’ or ‘bad’.

For example, tables (42%, Fig. 2(d)-middle), lists (9%), and detailed visualizations (88%) can provide very detailed information
Miniature charts (21%), on the contrary, are small and concise visualizations without axis descriptions, labels, or tickmarks.
Trend-arrows (13%) are small arrows pointing up/down and are used to indicate the direction of change in a data value.
Finally, numbers (62%) are numerical representations of individual values, placed prominently on a dashboard
Coding was done by two independent coders coding each dashboard independently. We disagreed on 32 dashboards (22%) but resolved all disagreement in discussion
Static Dashboard (21%)—By static dashboard, we refer to the traditional notion of a dashboard as a static (no-interaction), single page
Analytic dashboards (73%)—This genre is what Few would call a Faceted Analytic Display [21].

Analytic dashboards generally use complete visualizations and tables to show larger and more detailed data sets . Many of these views are fully interactive, providing for exploration , navigation , and drilldown .
Magazine Dashboards (2%)—Many dashboards relating to Covid-19, climate change, politics, etc were created by news agencies and similar media outlets.

From an information-theoretic perspective, a dashboard encodes a data space that is smaller than the data space of the data to be displayed.
Consider a time series representing the daily number of positive test cases for Covid-19 during a period of 500 days.

Reducing one of the parameters (screenspace, abstraction, number of pages, interaction) requires an increase in one of multiple of the other parameters.
Such parameters can be, e.g., abstraction, screenspace, number of pages, and interactivity. In a design process, the goal is to minimize each of these parameters.
The workshop ran for 2 weeks and was open to everyone with a dashboard design task at hand.
The entire workshop was held on Zoom, encouraging participants to work on their design mockups asynchronously
We had 23 participants in total from diverse backgrounds, including data science, medicine, psychology, economics, bioinformatics, design, etc.
About half of the participants had prior experience of one to several years in dashboard design with Power BI and Tableau.
Information overload was a frequent topic related to what information to include in a dashboard and how much information to include.

Eventually, the scope of this paper is not to suggest ‘good designs’, but to inform future studies.
